chapter: Trombone technique, plunger mute and the California years
title: Amos Gilliat, the toothless trombone virtuoso, and King Oliver selling clams
summary: Dickenson tells of a ragged trombonist who played an exercise book flawlessly without teeth, and of seeing King Oliver selling clams in Savannah.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Remembering King Oliver: the man, the band, the decline

blocks.x: You mentioned earlier -- you mentioned a man named Amos Gilliad (PHONETIC).
I was with Zack White's band. Zack White's band. And we went to Harrisburg, Pennsylvania, and we were at some hotel there. Some third class hotel -- fourth class hotel or something.

You know, we didn't have no money hardly. Scuffling you know. And here comes this guy. And he was real raggedy you know. And we had a chum along named Stump Brady. Stump incidentally is one of the -- was one of the best lead trombone players. He was really great and I hope he still can play anyhow.

He brought this guy around to the room and they had one of those Aubon (PHONETIC) books -- it's a big thing -- it's a book that you learn in that's got all the trombone things -- all the exercises and things that a trombone does. And this guy took -- took Stumpy's horn and played everything in tempo.
All the whole thing just like triple tones, double tones, and everything. And he didn't have no teeth.

And he didn't have no teeth. He played without any teeth. He didn't have none of them put in there. He just played. And played everything, the triple tone, the double tone, the whole bit. And he played it in tempo.

That's the greatest trombone player -- I mean as far as technique is concerned -- I've never seen anybody like that you know. Read the stuff just like that you know and run all through it. They tell me he was with a circus band years ago. I think it was James P. Lowry. Have you ever heard of that?

I think he was with him years ago. Amos Gayle (PHONETIC). He's a guy to be remembered. No one knows -- he was a street cleaner when he died. And just like -- just like King Oliver was selling clams or something on the street. You know. That's a damn shame. It's a shame. This guy should be remembered because they are great musicians. And you know KIng Oliver was a great musician. He was one of the great firsts.
Sure. Sure, I seen him down in Savannah, Georgia, I think. Savannah -- I think that's where he was at -- where I seen him. I was down there with the Blanche Calloway band.
And he was selling clams or something on the street, you know. What a great -- what a fall for a grand old man like that. You know --
It's strange when you think of it and he wasn't even that old. And it seemed that way then, but --
